PullRequest.Title: Automations: Scope list tool results to providers
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

- group `listAutomations` results by provider so catalogue state is scoped to the host it describes
- expose provider creation capability and per-Automation available operations to guide follow-up tool calls
- clarify model guidance so an unavailable provider does not make Automations from ready providers appear unavailable
- add focused coverage for ready and unavailable providers, visible incomplete rows, and configuration round trips

## Validation

- `npm run compile-client`
- targeted ESLint for the changed Automation tool files
- 41 focused Automation tool tests
- live Code OSS trial with GPT-5.6 Luna at medium thinking: created, edited, ran, and deleted an Automation while a second provider was unavailable

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed per-row calls and synchronous list invocation are direct. ProviderAutomationService.can* each calls findAutomationStore; findAutomationStore calls getStores/getProviders and probes stores with getAutomation, while AgentHostAutomationStore.getAutomation and can* each use a linear _findAutomationEntry scan. Exact latency depends on how many definitions and hosts users accumulate, so severity is low, but the quadratic mechanism is explicit and unbounded.
Findings.PerformanceResource: CPU work and temporary strings/descriptors created by repeated provider sorting, ID scans, URI/config projection, and capability-array construction.
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For N visible automations, the diff adds 3N aggregate capability queries; each scans registered provider stores and linearly searches catalogue entries, then the selected store linearly searches again. Effective work is quadratic in catalogue size, with extra repeated provider sorting as provider count grows.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased synchronous list-tool latency and CPU/GC pressure as catalogues grow.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The prior list implementation read the aggregate automation snapshot once, mapped each descriptor once, and serialized it, so work was linear in visible automations plus output bytes and made no per-row capability queries.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Each listAutomations invocation now performs canRunAutomation, canUpdateAutomation, and canDeleteAutomation through the aggregate service for every visible automation, adding repeated provider enumeration and catalogue scans to the synchronous tool path.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 1102 is the first of three new per-row calls to the aggregate IAutomationService capability methods; line 162 invokes this helper for every automation in every provider. The deleted implementation only mapped each aggregate automation through toAutomationToolOutput and performed no capability routing.
Findings.Title: Avoid re-routing every row's capabilities through the aggregate service
Findings.Impact: Invoking listAutomations with a catalogue accumulated to many definitions, especially across several local/remote Agent Hosts, synchronously burns CPU and allocations before the tool can return, increasing chat tool latency and GC pressure.
Findings.Evidence: toAutomationListToolOutput calls all three aggregate capability methods per row. ProviderAutomationService routes each call via findAutomationStore(), whose getStores() obtains and sorts providers and whose find() calls store.getAutomation(id). AgentHostAutomationStore.getAutomation() linearly scans catalog.entries and projects a descriptor; the subsequent store.can* call linearly scans the same entries again. Thus listing N definitions creates O(N^2) ID comparisons/string construction plus 3N discarded descriptor projections rather than a single catalogue pass.
Findings.Recommendation: Build operation metadata in one provider-local pass: expose or derive each entry's operation set from the owning store, or add an indexed/batched capability lookup, and pass that provider-local result into serialization instead of routing three aggregate can* calls per row.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: At the Eventually workbench phase, four tool instances and their metadata must be registered. The changed ListAutomationsTool constructor only resolves an in-memory service reference; provider catalogue projection and serialization remain off this path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant four tool registrations; independent of providers and automation count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous, constant-count tool construction and registration; no queue, limiter, or parallel work is involved.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Tool construction uses existing delayed/singleton services; no catalogue read or cache fill occurs during registration. The added provider-service reference does not initiate an Agent Host fetch.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the contribution constructor and service registrations that no filesystem, subprocess, IPC, database, or network operation is added to startup.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Instantiation-service overhead is not measured, but the changed dependency resolves a service already required transitively by IAutomationService and adds no scaling work.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable startup regression; the changed constructor dependency adds only in-memory DI resolution.

Scenarios.Scenario: Model invokes listAutomations with ready and unavailable local/remote Agent Host providers
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After the enabled-setting check, provider sorting, observable reads, per-automation projection/capability computation, counts, and JSON serialization all complete synchronously before the tool result returns. Existing AHP catalogue delivery is off path when ready; loading/unavailable providers return their current incomplete snapshot without awaiting the host.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Maintains the provider's authoritative AutomationState subscription whose latest local value backs observable reads.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One long-lived AHP catalogue subscription per connected Automation-capable provider, independent of automation row count and not created per list invocation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The aggregate IAutomationService snapshot consumed the same provider subscriptions before this diff; no additional AHP request or subscription was added.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the invocation critical path for ready providers; when no verified snapshot exists, the tool reports loading/unavailable state instead of awaiting network delivery.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serializes the provider-grouped catalogue as formatted JSON.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one JSON.stringify per list invocation over P provider records and N visible automation descriptors; payload bytes scale with all prompts/session templates plus small provider and operation metadata.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The prior tool also performed one formatted JSON serialization over all N aggregate automation descriptors, without provider records or availableOperations.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Serialization must finish before the tool result is returned to chat.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: P registered Automation providers and N total visible definitions, with no cross-provider deduplication because identities are provider-scoped. Required output transformation/serialization is O(N plus bytes); the added capability routing performs 3N queries whose scans yield quadratic catalogue work.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Fully serial synchronous work in the renderer. There is no limiter or coalescing because no asynchronous operation is dispatched; repeated model/tool invocations repeat the computation.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Each provider store exposes the latest observable catalogue snapshot. Ready and incomplete providers are read from that snapshot; listAutomations neither fetches nor waits, and unavailable/empty states are not negatively cached by this diff. Derived catalogue projections may be reused while unchanged, but the new aggregate capability queries are recomputed for every row and invocation.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: the changed map reaches three aggregate can* calls per visible row, and traced implementations synchronously enumerate/sort providers and linearly scan Agent Host catalogue entries. No new IPC/network call occurs per row.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Typical user catalogue size and prompt/template byte size are not bounded or measured. This uncertainty lowers the repeated-work finding to low severity; it does not change the proven quadratic lookup mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported the introduced per-row aggregate capability routing as low-severity repeated synchronous work. Provider grouping, incomplete-state handling, and the one serialization boundary otherwise add only linear metadata and no boundary fan-out.

Scenarios.Scenario: listAutomations invoked while Automations are disabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The disabled-setting guard returns an error result before getProviders, observable reads, capability checks, or serialization.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant, independent of provider and automation counts.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single synchronous constant-time guard; no asynchronous work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The configuration value is read once; no provider snapshot, capability state, or output serialization is accessed or cached.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the early return preceding all changed provider enumeration.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material; the branch is explicit.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression on this branch because all newly added work is bypassed.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over both changed files and all diff pages. Traced startup registration, enabled/disabled list invocation, provider catalogue ownership, AHP state delivery, serialization, capability routing, cache state, and concurrency. Submitted one low-severity repeated-work finding; found no new boundary fan-out, retention, eager startup work, or regression fix to record.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
